title: Ehud, left-handed (Judges 3:12–30)
hookLine: a left-handed man hides his sword where no one checks

lines: A TWO-EDGED BLADE, A CUBIT LONG.
cards: A short blade, two-edged, about a cubit long. A man straps it to his right thigh, under his clothes, and walks toward the palace of a king. He's carrying tribute, the payment his people owe to Moab.

Nobody stops him. A man bringing gifts to a king is easy to wave through. The book has already told us the one thing about him that matters here: "Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded."

teach.b: The dial turns exactly as promised. Israel does evil again. Eglon, king of Moab, takes the city of palm trees, and Israel serves him for eighteen years.
They cry out, and the Lord raises up a deliverer. His introduction isn't his strength, his family's fame or his faith. It's his left hand.
The text doesn't explain why that matters.
Some readers suggest guards would check a fighter's left side, where a right-handed man wears his sword; the story only tells us where Ehud hid his. Then it slows down.
Ehud delivers the tribute and leaves with the men who carried it.

teach.h: A SECRET WORD, A MESSAGE FROM GOD.
teach.b: At the carved stones near Gilgal he sends them on, turns back alone, and tells the king: I have a secret word for you. The king sends everyone out.
Alone in the king's private upper room, Ehud says: I have a message from God for you. The king rises from his seat, and with his left hand Ehud draws the blade.
The text tells the rest plainly and briefly: the king falls, Ehud locks the doors and slips out, and the servants wait outside, embarrassed, assuming the king needs privacy, until it's far too late.
By then Ehud is in the hill country of Ephraim, blowing the shofar. Follow me, he calls, and the people take the fords of the Jordan, and the land has rest.

teach.h: WHERE NO ONE THINKS TO LOOK.
teach.b: A man introduced by one overlooked detail goes where no one thinks to look. The thing that set him apart is the very thing that let him through.

how: Jews read the story of Ehud as part of Judges, among the Former Prophets; it follows soon after chapter two sets out the cycle of straying and rescue.

o: a guard in Eglon's palace who let the visitor in
the left-handed judge who freed Israel from Moab
the king of Moab who ruled Israel eighteen years

p: blown on the hills of Ephraim

s: Ehud is introduced by his strength and his well-known family
the text's one detail is that he was left-handed.
Eglon's servants waited outside, thinking the king wanted privacy
they waited until they were embarrassed, and then it was too late.
the text explains why being left-handed mattered
it only tells us where he hid the blade; the reason is left to readers.

games.q: you're Ehud. you've delivered Moab's tribute and you're heading home with the men who carried it. at the carved stones near Gilgal, what do you do?
o: keep walking home with the others.
send them on, and turn back alone.
go back with everyone to thank the king.
games.why: he sends them on, turns back alone, and tells the king he has a secret word for him. the blade is still on his right thigh.

practice: Bring to mind one thing about you that people tend to miss or count against you: being quiet, young or new, an accent, a different way of seeing, a skill nobody asks about. Hold it a moment without apologizing for it.
Then ask where it could be exactly what's needed, one room, one problem, one person, and let a picture come.

wordCard.voice: Ehud. Son of Gera, of Benjamin, a man lefthanded: the judge raised up when Israel cried out, who carried a blade where no one checked and blew the shofar on the hills of Ephraim. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Ehud, son of Gera, the Benjamite judge of Judges 3.

carryVoice: Your line: left-handed. The overlooked detail was the whole story. Day seven hundred eleven, done.
